newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: C&A says will defy AIRC recommendation.
newsitem.headline: C&A says will defy AIRC recommendation.

text.p: Coal and Allied Industries Ltd will press ahead with a continuous mining plan for the Hunter Valley No 1 mine north of Sydney despite a recommendation by the Australian Industrial Relations Commission (AIRC) that it should not do so, a company executive told Reuters on Tuesday.

In a day of fast-moving developments in the Hunter Valley coal mine dispute, Commissioner Greg Harrison issued a recommendation on Tuesday afternoon declaring Coal and Allied's decision to implement continuous mining "contrary to the spirit of previous recommendations of the commission".

Allan Davies, mine general manager of the Hunter Valley No 1 mine, told Reuters the recommendation had been given very careful consideration. "But in the end it was a business decision that we've made, not an industrial one, and so we're pressing ahead with the changes in the plant," he said.

Officials of the Construction, Forestry Mining and Energy Union, which earlier described the company's continuous mining plan for the mine as "a provocative action", were not immediately available for comment.
Davies said the company was not expecting the union to go on strike over the matter.
"Every week that this goes on, it's costing us about A$160,000, but frankly it's just important that the changes proceed simple because it's a good business decision," he said.
Commissioner Harrison's handwritten recommendation was issued to CFMEU officials on Tuesday after the company, controlled by Rio Tinto Plc/Ltd, announced its continuous mining plan.
It said: "On 18 August the company implemented work changes in the coal handling and preparation plant.

"In my opinion the implementation of these changes at this time is not conducive to the negotiations currently proceeding and are contrary to the spirit and intent of intent of previous recommendations of the commission.
"Accordingly the changes should be deferred for further consideration upon the expiry of current 21 day negotiating period."
In a statement after Harrison's recommendation was handed down, CFMEU vice-president Mick Kelly said Rio Tinto's plan to revert to continuous operations using staff was "not on".
The Hunter Valley No 1 mine produces about 25,000 tonnes of coal a day for Japanese and east Asian customers.
It was the target of a six week strike which was brought to an end on July 22 when the AIRC recommended that the company and the union negotiate for 21 days.
The AIRC averted the threat of a renewed strike on August 12 by recommending negotiations continue for a further 21 days.
Coal and Allied is about 70 percent owned by Rio Tinto.
